analysis.one_liner: Gives every state the full enhanced federal Medicaid match whenever it expands coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote; no state that had refused Medicaid expansion was affected.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Affordable Care Act, states that expanded Medicaid to low-income adults got extra federal money, but only if they expanded by a fixed calendar deadline — states that expanded late got less federal help. This bill would have given any state the same generous federal match (starting at 100% and stepping down to 90%) no matter when it expanded, and it would have applied retroactively. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured adults in states that had not expanded Medicaid — the bill would have made expansion much cheaper for their state governments, removing the main fiscal reason states cited for holding out. Hospitals in those states would also gain, because tens of thousands of newly insured patients means far less unpaid emergency care. State governments in non-expansion states would gain federal funds to cover most of the cost of expansion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured low-income adults in non-expansion states

how_it_helps.text: The bill keeps the ACA's enhanced federal match — 100% for the first three years, stepping down to 90% — but ties it to when a state actually expands rather than to fixed calendar years, so a late-expanding state gets the same deal as an early one [S3].
It applies retroactively, taking effect as if written into the original ACA, so a state expanding later would be paid as though it had expanded on time [S3].

The CRS summary confirms the enhanced federal medical assistance percentage (FMAP) would go to every state that expands Medicaid for the ACA newly eligible population, regardless of when the expansion takes place [S2].

Because the federal government would pick up 90% or more of expansion costs, the bill targets the argument state leaders used to refuse expansion — that their state would have to pay too much of the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear most of the new cost, since the bill pays 90–100% of coverage for newly enrolled adults in states that expand. Non-expansion states would still owe a small share of the cost of covering newly eligible adults once they signed on.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the federal government to pay the enhanced match indefinitely — it removes the fixed calendar endpoint and simply continues the 90% match for every succeeding quarter, an open-ended federal commitment [S3].
The retroactive effective date would apply new spending as if it had been law since 2010, a cost that grows with every state that newly expands [S3].
By making expansion essentially free to state budgets, the bill reduces state governments' reason to control enrollment costs, shifting long-term fiscal responsibility to Washington.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and well-targeted: the same ACA expansion that covered millions of people in adopting states, offered on the same federal financial terms to people in states that held out. The main honest objection is fiscal — the bill makes the 90% federal match permanent and retroactive rather than time-limited, which is an ongoing federal cost. On balance the bill does for late-expanding states exactly what the ACA did for early ones, so the parity argument is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Lewis of Georgia introduced the bill on January 30, 2019, joined by Reps. Terri Sewell of Alabama and Sanford Bishop of Georgia [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is where Medicaid legislation starts in the House [S5].
The bill drew six cosponsors, all Democrats, and the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the 116th Congress [S4].
The bill's action history shows only the introduction and the referral — no markup, no report, no floor vote — and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The uninsured adults in non-expansion states gained nothing, and continue to rely on a patchwork of emergency-room care. The outcome left the federal budget and non-expansion state budgets unchanged, while hospitals in those states continued to absorb unpaid care costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal and non-expansion state budgets; the uninsured lost

for.name: Rep. John Lewis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give late-expanding states the same enhanced federal Medicaid match as early expanders.

for.name: Reps. Terri Sewell and Sanford Bishop
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors; both represent states that had not expanded Medicaid.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 30, 2019 and never held a markup or reported it out; the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill drew no Republican support, but because it never got a hearing or a vote the record does not show how the full House would have split.

industries.note: Hospitals absorb the cost of care for uninsured patients, so the bill's failure means they keep bearing uncompensated-care costs. The public in those states loses coverage that hospitals had a financial stake in providing.

Each new state expansion enrolls hundreds of thousands of people in state Medicaid programs, often run through private managed-care insurers; the bill's death forecloses that new business. Insurers' gain here runs alongside the public's gain in coverage.

The bill would have offered these states a 90–100% federal match, making expansion nearly free; its death leaves state budgets unchanged but their residents uninsured. States also avoided any new long-term funding obligation.
